job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Iris Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my grandmother Ilona in her flat, so mornings start with her tea and the radio. I spend three or four hours on applications to councils, surveyors and construction firms, and on Saturdays I work at a hardware store, where I at least know what a coupling is. I print and tick off every application on a paper list, because that's how I keep track.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was the last stretch of study like, and what are you hoping for next?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did civil engineering and passed. My final project was a drainage study for a village road that floods every spring, and I measured the slopes myself. No internship, since the firms that offered places wanted people with higher marks, and I've sent about 55 applications and had one interview that went nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's sensible. Engineering is about checking things work, and I never trusted the claims. At work I'd say the tools save a few minutes with spreadsheets and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my situation stays the same. Councils are freezing hiring, and consultancies pick graduates with placements. I'm not going to be the person they notice, and that's what bothers me, not the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen the search to small surveying firms and contractors in towns within an hour's train ride. I'd ask for work experience for free for a month if that gets a reference, and keep the Saturday job. I'd also sit the exam for the site safety card, about 120 pounds, which many site jobs ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in a steady, flat way, like a dull toothache.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the safety card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's a thing you can show. It says I can walk on a site without being a risk. It's a real step, not another CV line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your grandmother say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandmother says get any job, any job, and wait for a better one. She came here with nothing and cleaned offices for thirty years, so she thinks I'm too fussy.

I'm not the person they notice, and that bothers me more than **technology**.
do: Widen the search to small **surveying** firms within an hour's train ride.
Ask for a month of unpaid **work experience** in return for a reference.
Pay about **120 pounds** for the site safety card exam.
feel: **Worried** in a steady, flat way, like a dull toothache.

fieldNote: Worry is about **hiring** and credentials, with AI barely mentioned.

steps.text: Apply to small surveying firms within an hour by train
Ask for a month of unpaid work experience for a reference
Sit the site safety card exam for about 120 pounds
Keep the Saturday shift at the hardware store

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people are getting a bit carried away, but I'd be careful. If the software checks designs and writes reports, firms will want fewer junior people. I'd say it to my friends and keep a lower profile at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the drawing, calculating and report checking that juniors do is the first thing to go. That's most of what graduate engineers do in their first two years. The site visits stay for longer, but those jobs go to people who've already got the experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to learn at least one of the design tools, and I'd hate it, because I like knowing what's inside a calculation. I'd take a weekend course, around 80 pounds, and look hard at roles that mix site and office, like inspection or quantity surveying. I'd keep the hardware store job for the cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sour. I've worked for something that's turning into something else while I'm still at the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bothers you about learning the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust a number I can't check by hand. In my project I verified every slope calculation twice. If a program gives me an answer, I want to know why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change that, if a job needed it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'm practical. I'd learn it and keep a hand-check habit on the side. But I'd be slower than people who used it all through uni.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe two years, but if it's true, nobody is prepared and that includes the government. I'd say it quietly, because I don't want to sound like a doom person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it'd be frightening. If AI does the thinking part of engineering better than any graduate, then the office jobs go. I'd have maybe three months of money, with my grandmother's flat as the only safety net, and she's seventy-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go after anything on a site: labouring, site assistant, a road crew. Robots for physical work come later, so that's the gap. I'd cut every extra, move none of my savings into anything risky, and ask my uncle in the building trade to take me on. And I'd go to the council to see what support exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, like carrying wet sand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't believe two years. Why plan for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the cost of being wrong is too big. If I plan and it doesn't happen, I've lost a little. If I don't plan and it does, I've lost everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your grandmother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay with her and keep paying my share of the bills. My grandmother can't move and I wouldn't leave. If things got bad, we'd manage on her pension and my wages together.

I'd say it quietly, because I don't want to sound like a **doom** person.
think: AI doing the thinking part of engineering better than any graduate would end the **office jobs**.

S2.quote: If I plan and it doesn't happen, I've lost a little. If I don't plan and it does, I've lost everything.
fieldNote: Plans for the **worst** while doubting it, a pragmatic centre response.
Sees the **gap** before robots reach site work.
Duty to her **grandmother** anchors her in place and limits options.

steps.text: Apply for labouring and site assistant jobs on road crews
Ask her uncle in the building trade for work
Visit the council to ask what support exists
Cut every extra expense and hold savings in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that the sensible people will work out what to do, and short enough that I should start. I'd say we need the construction trades and the engineers to keep working together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit better. If I can get a first job in a year, I'll have four years of site knowledge, and that's the kind of experience that's harder to replace. I'd feel I had a chance, if a slim one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any engineering-adjacent job, even a technician's job, and build up the safety card, a driving licence and a surveying qualification. I'd put 100 a month away. And I'd teach myself the design tools slowly, one a quarter, because I don't want to be last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight but workable. Like a hill I can see the top of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a driving licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most site and inspection jobs need one, and I don't have it yet. It's about 1,000 pounds all in and it's one of the few things that shows an employer I'm ready to be sent somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of those steps would you drop first if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The design tools course. I'd teach myself from free videos instead. The licence and the card are things employers look for, and no one asks for a certificate in the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for sensible planning, if people actually plan. I'd say councils and colleges should start building courses for it, not waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be anxious, but less. A decade gives me time to get a first job, then a second, and a professional qualification. The risk is I spend those years waiting for the door to open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying and keep the store job. I'd aim to be a chartered technician in about six years and learn new tools in small steps. I'd save about 150 a month and, with my grandmother's flat, think about a deposit. I'd stay close to people who work on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not calm, but easier. I can breathe in between the applications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in year three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm still in the same job and everyone else has moved up. Time to prepare only helps if you use it, and I know I can drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from other people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Employers who give a graduate a chance without a placement behind them. One yes would change a lot for me, and I'd work twice as hard for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd have no experience, little money and an elderly grandmother. What would help is employers taking on graduates without a placement, a way to get trade tickets cheaply, and honest forecasts so we can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume graduates are fussy. Mostly I'm just waiting for one person to say yes, and I'm ready to work harder than anyone to deserve it.

headlineQuote: Mostly I'm just waiting for one person to say yes, and I'm ready to work harder than anyone to deserve it.
portrait: Iris is a 23-year-old **civil engineering** graduate with a pass and no internship, about 55 applications sent.
She lives with her grandmother Ilona, works Saturdays at a **hardware store** and tracks applications on paper.
She is pragmatic, centre in her views and has never used AI tools, **distrusting** numbers she can't check.
Her mood stays **anxious** in most worlds and turns alarmed only when two years leave no time.
Her plans are practical and **site-based**: safety card, driving licence, technician work and family help.
biggestWorry: The **2028** case, with no experience, little money and an elderly grandmother to look after.
whatWouldHelp: Employers who hire without a **placement**, cheap trade tickets and honest forecasts.
